W4405407480.a1.text: The modal collapse argument claims divine simplicity forces God to necessarily create whatever He creates and creatures to necessarily perform their actions.
W4405407480.a1.quote: The modal collapse argument states that the traditional doctrine of divine simplicity entails that God necessarily creates whatever he creates and also that all creatures necessarily perform whatever actions they perform.

W4405407480.a2.text: Responding to modal collapse requires that part of the truthmaker linking God to contingent facts be extrinsic, locating contingency there.
W4405407480.a2.quote: Section 1 explains why responding to the modal collapse argument requires that part of the truthmaker relating God to contingent facts be extrinsic to God, and that it is only in this part that contingency lies.

W4405407480.a3.text: The paper defends a general view of action where such properties can be at least partially extrinsic.
W4405407480.a3.quote: This paper argues for a general view of action, in which such properties can turn out to be at least partially extrinsic.

W4405407480.c001.text: If God is simple, then God has no intrinsic accidental or contingent properties.
W4405407480.c001.quote: (i) If God is simple, God has no intrinsic accidental or contingent properties;

W4405407480.c002.text: It is an intrinsic property of God to have freely chosen to create the actual world and to know everything about the contingent individual creatures He creates.
W4405407480.c002.quote: (ii) it is an intrinsic property of God (a) to have freely chosen to create the actual world and (b) to know everything about the contingent individual creatures he creates;

W4405407480.c003.text: If God freely chooses to create the actual world, then it is contingent that God created it and that He created it exactly as He did.
W4405407480.c003.quote: (iii) if God freely chooses to create the actual world, it is contingent that God created it and that he created it exactly the way he created it;

W4405407480.c004.text: If individual creatures are contingently created by God, then any knowledge about them is knowledge of contingent facts and therefore a contingent knowledge.
W4405407480.c004.quote: (iv) if individual creatures are contingently created by God, any knowledge about them is a knowledge of contingent facts and therefore a contingent knowledge;

W4405407480.c005.text: Therefore the properties of freely choosing to create the world and knowing everything about contingent creatures are intrinsic properties that God contingently has.
W4405407480.c005.quote: (v) (a) and (b) are intrinsic properties that God contingently has;

W4405407480.c006.text: Therefore God has intrinsic accidental properties.

W4405407480.c008.text: The modal collapse argument is probably the most difficult objection to the doctrine of divine simplicity.
W4405407480.c008.quote: Among objections to the doctrine of divine simplicity (DDS) frequently discussed in recent literature, the so called “modal collapse argument” is probably the more difficult one.

W4405407480.c009.text: A satisfactory solution to the modal collapse argument requires a theory of volition and knowledge where properties (a) and (b) are extrinsic, thus denying premise (1)(ii).
W4405407480.c009.quote: A satisfactory solution to (1) requires a theory of volition and knowledge where properties (a) and (b), are extrinsic properties, i.e. denying premise (1)(ii).

W4405407480.c010.text: The asymmetry thesis states that the relationship from creature to creator is real, while the relationship from creator to creature is only of reason.
W4405407480.c010.quote: (2) Asymmetry thesis. The relationship that goes from the creature to the creator is real, but the correlative relationship that goes from the creator to the creature is only of reason.

W4405407480.c011.quote: If a is really related by R to b, but there is no foundation in b of the same type as a’s foundation for R to b, then there is no real corelation R’ in b, and R and R’ are non-mutual

W4405407480.c012.text: Divine simplicity requires that all non‑tautological truths only about God have only God himself as their minimal truthmaker.
W4405407480.c012.quote: divine simplicity requires that all non-tautological truths that are only about God, have only God himself as their minimal truthmaker (Pruss 2008, 152–54).

W4405407480.c013.text: Any correct attribution to God of an accidental property has as its truthmaker God and something contingent besides God, so the property is at least partially extrinsic.
W4405407480.c013.quote: any correct attribution to God of an accidental property has as its truthmaker God and something contingent besides God, and hence the property is at least in part extrinsic

W4405407480.c014.text: The truth of the proposition ‘God freely chooses to create the actual world’ depends on the conjunction of a necessary fact about God and a contingent fact about the world.
W4405407480.c014.quote: (4) Partial extrinsicness of divine volition of the contingent. What makes true the proposition “God freely chooses to create the actual world” is the conjunction of a necessary fact about God and a contingent fact about the world.

W4405407480.c015.text: God’s relation to the world is partially based on facts extrinsic to God, not on contingent intrinsic facts.
W4405407480.c015.quote: Partial extrinsicness of God's relation to the world. The relations between God and the world are at least partially based on facts that are extrinsic to God, and are not based on contingent facts intrinsic to God.

W4405407480.c016.text: God freely chooses to create the actual world because a necessary fact about God combines with a contingent fact about the world.
W4405407480.c016.quote: Partial extrinsicness of divine volition of the contingent. What makes true the proposition “God freely chooses to create the actual world” is the conjunction of a necessary fact about God and a contingent fact about the world.

W4405407480.c017.text: God knows the actions of free agents because a necessary fact about God combines with a contingent fact about created free agents.
W4405407480.c017.quote: Partial extrinsicness of divine knowledge of contingent particulars. What makes true the proposition “God knows the actions performed by free agents” is the conjunction of a necessary fact about God and a contingent fact about created free agents.

W4405407480.c018.text: Accepting hypotheses (4) and (5) denies that God possesses any accidental intrinsic properties.
W4405407480.c018.quote: Accepting hypotheses (4) and (5) entails denying (1) (ii), because (a) and (b) can turn out true without involving any accidental intrinsic properties of God whatsoever.

W4405407480.c019.text: The general hypothesis (3) lets us dismiss any other variant of the modal collapse argument.
W4405407480.c019.quote: Further on, the more general hypothesis (3) allows us to dismiss any other possible variant of the argument of modal collapse.

W4405407480.c020.text: Aquinas’ claim that cognitive and volitional acts are immanent makes (4) and (5) implausible because their truthmakers would have to be intrinsic to God.
W4405407480.c020.quote: However, there are some obvious reasons to consider (4) and (5) implausible. Aquinas himself is emphatic about the immanent character that cognitive and volitional acts have.

W4405407480.c021.text: We only need to show that volitional and cognitive acts are partially extrinsic, with contingency arising from external facts rather than God’s immanent act.
W4405407480.c021.quote: Let us remember, however, that we do not need to demonstrate that such volitional and cognitive acts are entirely extrinsic. Instead, we need only to show that they are partially so, and that the contingency involved arises solely from a contingent fact about the external object willed or known (not from the agent’s or knower’s immanent act).

W4405407480.c022.text: Causal relations always require a property in the effect, and a property in the cause only when the cause gains perfection from the effect.
W4405407480.c022.quote: Causal relations requiring real properties in both relata. Causal relations always require positing something within the effect (the acted, moved, or effected) but only require positing something in the cause (the mover, or the agent) when the latter obtains some perfection from the occurrence of the effect.

W4405407480.c023.text: Parsimony demands that we do not posit more real properties than are strictly necessary to ground a relation.
W4405407480.c023.quote: This idea can be defended on simple grounds of explanatory economics. Parsimony requires us not to posit any more real properties than those strictly necessary to properly ground the relation.

W4405407480.c024.text: Grant argues that assuming an intrinsic property of a cause either makes the effect non‑contingent or adds another contingent fact, undermining cosmological arguments.
W4405407480.c024.quote: Grant shows that if we assume that in order to make sense of a’s causally accounting for b there must be some real or intrinsic property or feature of a that would not be there were a not causing b, then this intrinsic feature or property of a must either be necessary or contingent.

W4405407480.c025.text: Defending DDS against (1) requires the same assumption needed to defend libertarian free will.
W4405407480.c025.quote: This last claim is important, because we must remember that vindicating libertarian free agency is one of the main motivations frequently invoked for the rejection of DDS.

W4405407480.c026.text: To overcome difficulty (1) we must extend the gratuitousness of God’s creative act to its ultimate consequences.
W4405407480.c026.quote: Therefore, in order to overcome difficulty (1), instead of denying the absolutely gratuitous character of God’s creative act, what we have to do is to carry this gratuitousness to its ultimate consequences.

W4405407480.c027.text: The precise content of a volitional act need not be an intrinsic feature of the agent.
W4405407480.c027.quote: There are good reasons to think that the precise content of a volitional act need not be an intrinsic feature of the agent.

W4405407480.c028.text: For any agent, the truthmaker of a free choice is the conjunction of an intrinsic desire and an extrinsic fact about the produced effect.
W4405407480.c028.quote: Partial extrinsicness of any volition. For any agent a who freely produces an effect x, the truthmaker of the proposition “a freely chooses to produce x” is the conjunction between (i) an intrinsic fact about a, consisting in the internal desire of end q, that can be equally fulfilled by performing a range of various actions, one of which involves producing x; (ii) a fact about x, consisting in the production of x being the precise action freely performed by a.

W4405407480.c029.text: (7)(ii) is a fact extrinsic to the agent and can be contingent without undermining God's absolute simplicity.
W4405407480.c029.quote: (7)(ii) is a fact extrinsic to the agent and can therefore be contingent without undermining God’s absolute simplicity.

W4405407480.c030.text: God's volition to create the world is not a causal relationship where the cause attains perfection from the effect, as described in scenario (6).
W4405407480.c030.quote: The key point to keep in mind is that this is not one of the scenarios described in (6)—a type of causal relationship where the cause attains a certain perfection from the occurrence of the effect.

W4405407480.c031.text: Aquinas holds that in a single act of volition God wills his own essence and also wills creatures, ordering the latter to the former as manifestations of his goodness, not because they contribute to his perfection.
W4405407480.c031.quote: Thomas Aquinas considered that in a single act of volition God wills his own essence and also wills the creatures. He wills the latter ordered to the former, and not insofar as they contribute in some way to his own perfection, but rather as manifestations of his goodness.

W4405407480.c032.text: Miller argues that situation (c) most resembles God's volitional act, where objects are willed as ordered to one another as manifestations rather than as independent means or ends.
W4405407480.c032.quote: Miller argues that situation (c) is the one that most resembles God’s volitional act.

W4405407480.c034.text: If God's purpose in loving creatures is sharing his goodness, any world could fulfill it, so the particular world created does not require a new volitional act; its contingency makes it the object of the necessary divine volition.
W4405407480.c034.quote: If God’s purpose in loving creatures is sharing his own goodness, this purpose could be perfectly fulfilled by creating a world completely different from ours, or even without any world being created at all.

W4405407480.c035.text: The description is compatible with Aquinas's claim that divine willing of contingent creatures includes their contingency.
W4405407480.c035.quote: This description is compatible with Aquinas’s claim that divine willing of contingent creatures includes their contingency (e. g., Summa Theologiae I q.19 a.8).

W4405407480.c036.text: Aquinas does not argue that the particular contingent creatures created by God are included in God's internal volition; only the general contingent nature is.
W4405407480.c036.quote: When claiming so, Aquinas does not argue that the particular contingent creatures created by God are included in God’s internal volition.

W4405407480.c037.quote: In my argument, the contingency of the effect is due to indeterminacy in the prior volition and does not require any concurrent secondary causes.

W4405407480.c038.text: One might argue that God's love must reach each creature's unique individuality, implying something within God beyond the single necessary love of his essence.
W4405407480.c038.quote: Someone might argue that God’s love for creatures is meant to reach them in their unique individuality, and therefore involves positing within God something more than the single necessary love of his own essence which manifests itself by extending indistinctly to the entire universe of possible creatures through which God could have freely shared his goodness.

W4405407480.c039.quote: All of this can be compatible with DDS as long as we insist that the energeiai do not posit an intrinsic contingent property on God himself, but simply modify his love intentionally by referring it to a concrete object as terminus of the loving relation.

W4405407480.c040.quote: Should such considerations lead us to conclude that God cannot know contingent individuals?

W4405407480.c041.text: Partial extrinsicness of divine speculative knowledge holds that 'God knows x' is true when (i) an intrinsic necessary fact about God exists and (ii) x exists as a particular creature.
W4405407480.c041.quote: (8) Partial extrinsicness of divine speculative knowledge. Whenever God knows a particular creature x, what makes true the proposition “God knows x” is the conjunction between (i) an intrinsic necessary fact about God, consisting in the divine essence being such as to speculatively know whatever happens to be the case without suffering any intrinsic change depending on the precise content of his knowledge; and (ii) a fact about x, consisting in x being the case, and therefore x being among those things that God knows.

W4405407480.c042.text: Partial extrinsicness of any fabricative knowledge holds that 'a knows x' is true when (i) the agent has intrinsic self‑knowledge including the chosen effect and (ii) x is the precise effect the agent freely produced.
W4405407480.c042.quote: (9) Partial extrinsicness of any fabricative knowledge. W4405407480.c043.text: Fabricative knowledge is possible because intentionally producing something gives the producer a certain knowledge of that thing.
W4405407480.c043.quote: Fabricative knowledge is possible because the intentional production of something grants a certain knowledge of it.

W4405407480.c044.quote: The existence of this knowledge that is not speculative-observational was lucidly defended by Anscombe (1963), and it constitutes a central element in both Aristotelian and Thomistic thought.

W4405407480.c045.quote: However, it is obvious that musicians know all the notes already played, since otherwise they would not know which note to play next. This knowledge of the part of the piece played so far does not have an observational source but arises from the very performance of the action.

W4405407480.c046.quote: Human agents lack full self‑transparency regarding their own actions: They have partial awareness of the concrete choices they have made, but they never have complete knowledge of the precise effects brought about by their decisions.

objections.text: Consider Ada, a potter who has always been disposed to make bowls and who, on a given morning, freely decides to make a bowl rather than a jug. The proposition 'Ada freely decides to make a bowl' is true. Its truth seems to depend on Ada's standing necessary-looking dispositions, but also on the contingent fact that she has clay and a wheel. Suppose we ask what makes the proposition true. A tempting answer is that the clay fact is merely a condition on what she can act upon, not a truthmaker for the decision itself. Now transfer this to God: 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' is true in virtue of God's will, with the world figuring only as the object willed. The world's contingency enters the content of the proposition (what is chosen) but not its truth-grounds (that God wills it). The proposition is therefore grounded entirely in God's intrinsic volition, and the claimed conjunction of a necessary fact about God with a contingent fact about the world is not required.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c014 fails because it assumes the truthmaker of 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' must include a contingent worldly fact, when the world figures only in the proposition's content (what is chosen), not in what makes the choice-attribution true.

objections.text: A necessarily existing being named Ash satisfies divine simplicity: every truth only about him has him alone as minimal truthmaker. Ash freely forms the contingent intrinsic intention to create world W. The relational proposition “Ash is the creator of W” is true solely because of that intrinsic contingent volition; W’s existence is an effect, not a partial metaphysical ground. If Ash had refrained, no relation would obtain, yet the relation that does obtain is wholly fixed by a contingent intrinsic fact, with no extrinsic fact partially constituting it.
objections.premise_fails_because: W4405407480.c015 fails because a simple being’s relation to its creation can be wholly grounded in a contingent intrinsic volition rather than in any extrinsic fact.

objections.text: God is absolutely simple—no parts, no accidents, essence identical to existence. Consider the proposition "God is unsurpassable in power." This is non-tautological and only about God: it is a single-subject predication naming no other entity. Yet its minimal truthmaker is not God alone. What makes it true is God plus the fact that no possible being exceeds God's power—a modal-comparative fact about the space of possible beings. If some possible being had possessed greater power, the proposition would be false, so its truthmaker must include the absence of such a being. Divine simplicity is a thesis about God's internal metaphysical composition; it says nothing about what entities serve as truthmakers for truths about God. A simple God can be the truthmaker for "God is powerful" without being the sole truthmaker for "God is unsurpassably powerful."
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W4405407480.c012 fails because divine simplicity concerns God's internal composition, not truthmaker relations, so it does not require that every non-tautological truth about God has only God as its minimal truthmaker.

objections.text: Imagine a theistic tradition where divine simplicity is defined in purely negative terms (e.g., ‘God is not composite’), and its adherents find modal collapseobjections incoherent because their notion of simplicity lacks the strong truthmaker commitments of premise c012. In this tradition, the modal collapse argument is not even a live issue, as the objection assumes a framework they reject. Thus, the argument’s difficulty is not universal.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c008 fails because the modal collapse argument is not the most difficult objection for all accounts of divine simplicity.

objections.text: Consider God's accidental property: 'being, at time t, the sole truthmaker of the world's existence.' In a world where God does not create, this property is absent; in our world, it is present. The property is therefore accidental. Now ask: what makes the attribution 'God is the sole truthmaker of the world's existence' correct? The answer is God alone—God's own nature as the creator. No contingent fact 'besides God' enters the truthmaking. The world's existence is not a further truthmaker alongside God; it is what God's truthmaking activity produces, not what constitutes the truth of the attribution. The attribution's truth is fixed by God's being the creator, full stop. Yet c013 insists that any correct attribution of an accidental property to God requires, as truthmaker, 'God and something contingent besides God.' This case shows an accidental property of God whose truthmaker is God alone, with no extrinsic contingent element. The property is accidental without being extrinsically grounded.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c013 fails because God's accidental property of being the sole truthmaker of the world's existence is correctly truthmade by God alone, with no contingent fact besides God required, contradicting the claim that accidental properties always need an extrinsic contingent truthmaker.

objections.text: Consider a scenario where God's volition to create the world is an intrinsic property, driven by God's own nature and desires. In this case, God's relation to the world is still partially based on facts extrinsic to God, such as the world's existence and properties. However, the accidental property of volition remains intrinsic to God, as it is a fundamental aspect of God's character. This scenario suggests that the connection between God's relation to the world and the nature of accidental properties is not as straightforward as assumed.
objections.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it incorrectly assumes that God's relation to the world being partially based on extrinsic facts necessarily implies that the accidental properties of volition and knowledge must also be extrinsic.

objections.text: Father John, a parish priest, teaches that God freely chose to create the actual world only because the world could be ordered in a certain way; he says God's will depends on the existence of contingent possibilities. In Thomist thought, God's free act of creation is a simple, non‑composite act whose truthmaker is God alone. The act does not require a contingent fact to be true; it is a necessary act of the divine intellect and will. Hence the proposition ‘God freely chooses to create the actual world’ cannot be true by virtue of a conjunction of a necessary fact and a contingent fact: it is true solely by God’s simple act, independent of any extrinsic condition.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise W4405407480.c014 fails because Thomist classical theism holds that God’s free act of creation is a simple, intrinsic act, not dependent on any contingent fact.

objections.text: Consider a person, Leo, who decides to drink water. The truth of 'Leo decides to drink water' is made true by Leo's internal volition. This volition is a property of Leo. The truthmaker is not Leo plus an external, contingent fact; the truthmaker is simply Leo, as a person possessing that specific mental state. Similarly, God's volition is a real, distinct attribute of His personhood. The contingency resides within the property God possesses, not in a fact that exists 'besides' Him. Therefore, an accidental property is not an extrinsic addition but an intrinsic part of God's person.
objections.premise_fails_because: W4405407480.c013 fails because a contingent property is held by the person and does not require a truthmaker existing 'besides' that person.

objections.text: A proponent of divine simplicity distinguishes between the truth-conditions of a proposition and the ontological nature of the properties it describes. For example, the truth of the proposition 'God chooses to create the world' depends on the contingent existence of the world, but the property of volition remains an intrinsic, necessary aspect of God's essence. The presence of an extrinsic truth-maker for a proposition does not necessitate that the property being predicated is an extrinsic attribute of the subject. W4405407480.c013 fails because it conflates the extrinsic truth-conditions of a proposition with the intrinsic nature of the property itself.

objections.text: Consider a case: God, eternally and without any change in His nature, wills that a certain lamp be lit at noon. The willing is intrinsic to God and grounded wholly in His necessary goodness and power. Now suppose a contingent fact about the world: the lamp's wick happens to be dry. The proposition 'God wills the lamp is lit' is true only if the lamp is lit, so its truthmaker includes a contingent fact about the wick. Yet the volition is not extrinsic in the relevant sense: had the wick been wet, God's willing would be unchanged and only its satisfaction, not the volition, would differ. The premise assumes that any contingent item in a truthmaker makes the property extrinsic, but the property's intrinsic character (the act of willing, individuated by God's nature) is fixed without the wick. The contingent fact enters only the truthmaker of the relational or satisfaction-involving proposition, not of the volition itself. So the antecedent of r1 can hold while the property remains intrinsic.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise r1 fails because it treats the presence of a contingent fact in a truthmaker for a volitional attribution as sufficient for extrinsicness, when the contingent fact may ground only a satisfaction condition of the willing, leaving the volition itself intrinsic to God.

objections.text: Consider God's actual volition V: God wills that Eve be created at t. Nothing in the world supplies the variation between V and some alternative volition V', in which God wills that Eve never exist. The world does not select which act occurs; the act itself is a distinct intrinsic state that could have been otherwise. In a world where God instead has V', the truthmaker for 'God wills an Eve-creating act' is V' itself. The variation is therefore supplied by which volitional state God is in, a non-world factor, and it is intrinsic to God. r2 treats 'not supplied by the world' as entailing 'content fixed necessarily,' which skips this option. The actual content is contingent, its variation is internal, and the modal collapse does not follow from that disjunct.
objections.premise_fails_because: The second disjunct of r2 wrongly infers that if variation is not supplied by the world, the act's content must be fixed necessarily, ignoring that the variation can be supplied by which intrinsic volitional state obtains.

objections.text: Consider Ada, a potter who has resolved to make one bowl and no other, before any clay exists. Her resolve is fixed by her settled character and plan; the content 'make bowl B' is picked out by her intention alone, and B's specific identity is not yet anything. When clay is delivered, B comes to exist, and the sentence 'Ada made B' becomes true. Her intention did not change; what changed is that a contingent object now satisfies a description her intrinsic intention already determined. The truthmaker of 'Ada made B' includes B, yet the content of her volition, 'make the bowl that suits this plan,' was fixed without reference to any worldly fact. Analogously, God's volition can have a content specified intrinsically, such as 'bring about whatever world satisfies this plan,' with the identity of W entering only in the truth of 'God creates W,' not in the content of the volition. The revised premise conflates the truthmaker of an attribution with the determinant of the volition's content, and the case shows these come apart.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise arg1.r3 assumes that the volition's content must be partly fixed by a contingent worldly fact, but Ada's case shows a volition can have a purely intrinsic content whose satisfaction, not its specification, requires an extrinsic object.

restatements.plain_english: Just because a true sentence about God's wanting something needs some outside fact to be true does not mean God's wanting itself depends on that outside fact. Suppose God wants a lamp to be lit. Whether the sentence 'God wants the lamp lit' is true depends on whether the lamp really gets lit, and that depends on the wick being dry. But God's wanting is the same either way: if the wick were wet, God would want the same thing, and only the outcome would be different. So the outside fact changes what is true about the wanting, not the wanting itself.

restatements.paper_vocabulary: Against revised premise r2 of the modal collapse argument (W4405407480.arg1.r2), which equates 'the variation is not supplied by the world' with 'the act's content is fixed necessarily': the disjunct is false because God's volitional state V' itself, an intrinsic and contingent divine state distinct from the actual volition V, supplies the variation between alternative divine acts, so the actual content of the volition can be contingent while its variation is internal to God and the modal collapse does not follow.
restatements.plain_english: The argument says that if the world isn't what makes God's choice different from the other choices God could have made, then God's choice must be fixed no matter what. That's wrong, because God could be in a different inner state, with a different choice inside it. What changes the choice is God's own inner state, not anything outside God, so the choice can be up to God and not fixed in advance.
restatements.neighboring_tradition: In the free-will and divine-freedom debates this is a reply to a dilemma about the source of contingency: it denies the exhaustive disjunction (contingency comes either from the world or from necessity) by adding a third option, internal variation in the agent's own volitional state, much as libertarian accounts of agency locate the source of alternative possibilities in the agent rather than in external circumstances, and as theists answering the Euthyphro-style or hiddenness-style dilemmas reject a forced choice between external determination and necessitarian fixing of the act.

rounds.speaker: referee
rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks the unstated premise as stated. The premise claims that if God's relation to the world is partially based on extrinsic facts, then the accidental properties (volition and knowledge) must be extrinsic. The objection provides a counterexample scenario in which God's relation to the world is partially extrinsic yet volition remains intrinsic, thereby challenging the conditional link the premise asserts. This is an attack on the premise itself, not a misreading.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: Under the argument's own truthmaker notion, the scenario is not coherent. You grant that the truthmaker of 'God wills to create the world' includes the world's existence. c013 says any correct attribution of an accidental property has God and something contingent besides God as truthmaker, and that makes the property at least partially extrinsic. Calling volition 'intrinsic' because it flows from God's nature is a different notion, one that c012 does not use. Your point that God's relation to the world is partly extrinsic (c015) does not by itself settle the status of volition, and the mp as written is too weak: it treats the relation as if it were the property. The bridge has to say that the volitional property is the very property whose truthmaker includes a contingent fact. c034 gives the best defence here: the necessary volition has the contingent world as its object, not as an intrinsic feature, so the contingency enters through the object and the property stays extrinsic. The argument survives, but only with the bridge made explicit. [W4405407480.c012] [W4405407480.c013] [W4405407480.c034] [W2737654126.a2]
rounds.revised_premise: An accidental property of God is extrinsic whenever its correct attribution has a contingent truthmaker besides God, so that volition and knowledge are extrinsic whenever they are correctly attributed to God in virtue of the contingent world.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You argue that the scenario I presented is incoherent under the argument's truthmaker notion, and that calling volition 'intrinsic' because it flows from God's nature is a different notion. However, you haven't addressed the core of my objection: that the connection between God's relation to the world and the nature of accidental properties is not as straightforward as assumed. You've focused on the technical aspects of truthmakers and property attribution, but haven't shown why the intrinsic nature of volition, driven by God's own nature and desires, couldn't be compatible with God's relation to the world being partially based on extrinsic facts. This distinction still seems plausible, and the argument's reliance on a straightforward connection between these concepts remains questionable.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that the argument's mp is not yet tight, and I concede that much. But your scenario does not show the gap you need. You say volition is intrinsic because it flows from God's nature and desires. The argument's notion is different: a property is intrinsic only if its minimal truthmaker is God alone [W4405407480.c012]. A property that flows from God's nature can still have as truthmaker God plus the contingent world, as in the case of God's willing this world rather than another, and c013 then makes it at least partially extrinsic. Your scenario only works if the world's existence drops out of the truthmaker of 'God wills to create this world', and you have not shown that. Your point that the relation is partly extrinsic (c015) is compatible with volition being intrinsic only if the relation and the volition come apart, and you have given no reason to think they do. The reply that God's necessary volition takes the contingent world as its object, not as an intrinsic feature, is the best route for the defender [W4405407480.c034]. Yet the object-based route also faces the worry that God is not simple if the object enters the truthmaker. So the argument needs the bridge stated explicitly. Still, the objection does not refute it. I concede that the mp as written is too weak and that the bridge is the real point at issue.

Revised premise: If the truthmaker of God's accidental volitional property includes a contingent fact about the world, then that property is extrinsic to God, whatever its origin in God's nature.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
You are right that extrinsic relations do not by themselves entail extrinsic properties in general. However, the argument does not rest on that broad entailment alone. The paper explicitly states that any accidental property attributed to God has as its truthmaker both God and something contingent besides God, making it at least partially extrinsic [W4405407480.c013]. The proposition that God freely chooses to create the actual world depends precisely on a conjunction of a necessary fact about God and a contingent fact about the world [W4405407480.c014]. Your scenario of a purely intrinsic accidental volition therefore conflicts with this truthmaker analysis. The extrinsic facts about the world do not merely accompany God's relation to the world [W4405407480.c015]; they enter into the minimal truthmaker for the volition itself. That said, the unstated premise overstates the case as a general entailment from extrinsic relations to extrinsic properties, and the argument should instead rest directly on the truthmaker overlap between the relation and the accidental property.

Revised premise: The same contingent facts about the world that partially ground God's relation to the world also belong to the minimal truthmaker for God's accidental volition and knowledge regarding that world, so these properties are at least partially extrinsic.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks premise c014 as stated. c014 claims that the truth of 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' depends on a conjunction of a necessary fact about God and a contingent fact about the world. The objection denies exactly this, arguing instead that the proposition is true solely by God's simple act, independent of any extrinsic condition. This is a straightforward rejection of the premise as written, not an attack on a different or distorted version of it.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: Father John's view is a serious rival, but it does not show that c014 is false; it shows that c014 is contested. The argument needs only that the truthmaker of the proposition includes something beyond God. Your objection says the act is simple and its truthmaker is God alone. Yet the modal collapse argument is aimed at the Thomist who holds that God's free choice is simple, and the question is whether the truthmaker for 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' can be God alone without collapse. If it can, then the proposition is true without any contingent fact, and the free choice cannot be contingent in the way c003 requires. That is exactly the dilemma the argument presses. The literature gives a route here: a truthmaker view on which God alone is the truthmaker for divine predicates [W7172336769.c066] would seem to back Father John, but it does so by making the predicate's truth independent of the world, which is what c013 and c015 deny for accidental predicates. Father John's contingency-of-possibilities gloss ('God's will depends on the existence of contingent possibilities') also concedes the point: a will that depends on a contingent condition is no longer solely God's simple act. So the objection pushes toward a view on which the act is free but its truthmaker is necessary, and the modal collapse worry returns: if the truthmaker is God alone and God is necessary, the creative choice is necessary. I therefore do not concede that c014 fails. The conjunctive claim is the argument's best reading of how contingency enters, and the objector's alternative is the collapse horn restated.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You have not shown that the truthmaker of “God freely chooses to create the actual world’’ must be a conjunction of a necessary fact and a contingent fact. The move from “God is the sole truthmaker’’ to “the proposition is true only by virtue of a necessary‑contingent conjunction’’ is unwarranted. Even if God is a necessary being, the proposition can be true of a world in which God’s simple act of choosing is instantiated and false of a possible world in which God’s simple act is instantiated differently. The modal status of the proposition depends on the content of the act, not on the modal status of its truthmaker. Thus the claim that the truthmaker “includes something beyond God’’ remains unsupported; you have merely restated the premise you are supposed to prove. Consequently c014 is still vulnerable to my objection.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: Your rejoinder is right that the step from 'God is the sole truthmaker of the act' to 'the proposition is true only through a necessary-contingent conjunction' needs more support than I gave it, and I should not have treated the dilemma as settled by the truthmaker view [W7172336769.c066]. But you have also shifted the modal question. You say the proposition's modal status depends on the content of the act, not on its truthmaker. That is a claim about which proposition is true at which world, and it still needs an account of why the content of God's simple act varies across worlds while God's intrinsic nature does not. Father John's gloss, that God's will depends on contingent possibilities, is exactly what supplies that variation, and it places a contingent fact in the truth-conditions of the proposition. If the variation is supplied by the world, then c014's conjunction is the right structure. If it is not, the act's content is fixed necessarily and the modal collapse returns, as the source note on the collapse objection anticipates [W4313406459.a1]. So I hold c014 against your rejoinder, but only in a weaker form than I first stated, which I now state as the revised premise.
rounds.revised_premise: The truth-conditions of 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' must include a contingent fact about the world that varies the content of God's otherwise necessary volition across possible worlds.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
You are right that Thomist metaphysics treats creation as a simple act whose truthmaker is God alone, but the argument concerns the truth of the *proposition* 'God freely chooses to create the actual world,' which is a contingent relational truth that is false unless the actual world exists [W4405407480.c014, W4405407480.c003]. The simplicity of the act does not entail that the proposition about the act lacks a contingent relatum; even a simple volition for *this* world requires the world's existence to make the proposition true [W4405407480.c016]. However, your objection lands partly: the argument as stated does not explicitly block the Thomist move of collapsing the proposition's truthmaker into God's simple act alone. To save the premise, we must add that a contingent relational proposition about God's free choice requires the contingent relatum as part of its truthmaker regardless of the act's internal simplicity.

Revised premise: The truth of the contingent relational proposition that God freely chooses to create the actual world requires the existence of the actual world as a truthmaker, even if God's act of will is metaphysically simple.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks c013 as stated. c013 claims that any correct attribution to God of an accidental property has as its truthmaker God and something contingent besides God, making the property at least partially extrinsic. The objection counters by arguing that the truthmaker is simply God himself possessing an intrinsic volitional property, with contingency residing within the property rather than in something external. This is a direct assault on c013's claim about the structure of the truthmaker, not an attack on a premise the argument does not hold or a different conclusion.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: The argument does not say God's volition is a foreign addition or a separate item from His person. Its claim, in c013 and c014, is that the truth of 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' requires a contingent fact about the world as part of its truthmaker. Leo's case shows only that a mental state can be the truthmaker of a volitional proposition with Leo alone as truthmaker, but Leo's volition is not in the same position: the proposition 'Leo decides to drink water' is about a volition whose object is fixed by Leo's act, while God's volition, on the argument's own c014, is about a particular world whose contingent character is supplied from outside God. You are right that the contingency can reside in the property, but the argument's question is whether the content of the act is fixed by God alone. If it is, the modal collapse returns, as the revised r2 premise states. So the objection shows that intrinsic volition is coherent in principle, which the argument can grant, without showing that God's volition, with its world-directed content, has God alone as minimal truthmaker. The c034 point, that the world is the object of a necessary volition, sits uneasily with the claim that the contingent object is supplied within God. I cannot fully rebut this: a defender of simplicity could say the contingency of the object is in God's will as a relation to whatever is willed, and that would make the property intrinsic in the sense Leo's case illustrates. Compare the simplicity-friendly reading in [W4229080938.c004] and [W4413414430.a2]; neither settles whether the world-relative content is intrinsic. The argument survives only if the premise that the variation is supplied by the world is kept as an extrinsic relation of the volition's content, which is what r1 says.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You attempt to evade my objection by bifurcating God’s volition into an "act" and its "content," claiming the content must be supplied by the world to avoid modal collapse. This relies on a false dichotomy. If the content of the volition—the specific, contingent object willed—is an intrinsic feature of the volitional property itself, then the truth of "God wills X" depends solely on God and His specific, contingent state. You argue that if the content is fixed by God, modal collapse returns, but this assumes that an intrinsic property cannot be contingent. By insisting that the "content" must be an external truthmaker to prevent modal collapse, you are essentially presupposing the extrinsicality you aim to prove. If the content is a feature of the property, the truthmaker remains God alone.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that the argument must show more than that intrinsic volition is coherent, and I grant that Leo's case establishes only that. But your rejoinder moves the burden to the wrong place. You say that a contingent content can be an intrinsic feature of the property, so the truthmaker remains God alone. The argument's premise c014 is precisely that the truth of 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' depends on a contingent fact about the world, and nothing in your rejoinder shows that this dependence is absent. Calling the contingency 'a feature of the property' relabels the world-directed content without saying what makes that content contingent if not the world. The modal collapse worry is not presupposed by me; it is the independent constraint that, if the content were fixed by God's nature alone, the act would be necessary (r2). You can avoid collapse only by making the content contingent in a way God's nature does not fix, and that contingency has to come from somewhere outside God's simple nature. The simplicity-friendly responses in [W4229080938.c004] and [W4413414430.a2] address the personhood and self-existence of God, not whether a world-relative content is intrinsic, so they do not decide the question. I cannot rule out a defender who says the relational content is intrinsic in the way Leo's case illustrates, but that defender must then deny c014 or accept that God's volition has a contingent truthmaker outside Him, which is the extrinsicality the argument asserts.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content: You assume God stands to His volition as Leo stands to his mental states: a substance bearing a distinct internal property. But the argument assumes divine simplicity, which denies that God is a substratum distinct from His act of will. If the variation in God's choice were located entirely within an intrinsic property identical to God, then either God is contingent or—since God is necessary—His volitional content is fixed across every world and modal collapse follows [W4405407480.arg1.r2]. That is why the argument holds that the truth of 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' depends on a conjunction of a necessary fact about God and a contingent fact about the world [W4405407480.c014]; the contingency is supplied by the world, not by a distinct internal state. Your analogy works for non-simple agents whose mental states are particulars distinct from them, but for a simple being the truthmaker of an accidental attribution must include something contingent besides God [W4405407480.c013]. The property is genuinely attributed to God, yet it remains partially extrinsic because its minimal truthmaker is God-plus-world.

rounds.content: You have not answered my objection; you have simply asserted that my position is untenable because it leads to the very problem we are discussing. You claim that if the contingency is intrinsic, modal collapse follows, and if it is not, simplicity is lost. By retreating to an "extrinsic" model to avoid modal collapse, you are not refuting my claim that the property could be intrinsic; you are merely conceding that the entire debate rests on whether that contingency can be contained within God's own identity.

The argument's c014 says the proposition 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' has a necessary fact about God and a contingent fact about the world as its conjunctive ground. Your Ash case replaces this with a single intrinsic volition whose object is fixed in the volition itself. If the object is fixed intrinsically and independently of W, the act's content is necessary and modal collapse returns (r2). If the object is fixed only by the world's actual character, then the truthmaker for 'Ash is the creator of W' includes W, and c015 holds. Your dilemma is therefore not a counterexample to c015 but a choice between the two horns the argument already names. [W4310750024.a3] shows a deterministic causal link is compatible with simplicity, but causal dependence is not truthmaking, as you rightly say, so it does not favour your picture. If the answer is God's nature alone, then the content is necessary and modal collapse returns, which the argument already identifies. If the answer includes the world, the property has an extrinsic constituent. The literature offers the extrinsic model of divine knowing, which claims there is no intrinsic change in God [W1967680842.a3], and a truthmaker view on which God alone is the truthmaker for divine predicates [W7172336769.c066]. Both are versions of your position, and both must face the r2 dilemma. rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content:
You claim that if the world fixes the content of God's volition, the property becomes extrinsic. However, you are conflating intentional content with ontological constitution. A property can be intrinsically necessary and simple while its intentional object is contingent. For instance, a necessary desire for a contingent object does not make the desire itself an extrinsic property; the property is the internal state, while the object is merely the referent.

By insisting that "fixing the content" requires an "extrinsic constituent," you assume that intentionality necessitates ontological composition. I contend that God’s volition is a simple, intrinsic property whose *object* is contingent. This allows for a contingent world without making the volitional property itself extrinsic or necessitating that the volition's content be a necessary fact. You have not shown why an intrinsic property cannot relate to a contingent object without being composed of it.

But your intentional-content model does not avoid the argument's real pressure. You say God's volition is a simple intrinsic state whose object W is contingent. The question is what makes the state a volition of W rather than of some other world. If the state is individuated by its object, then the object-relation is part of the property's identity, and a property whose identity is partly fixed by a contingent relatum is extrinsic in the sense the argument uses, even if the relatum is not a constituent. If instead the state is individuated by God's nature alone, then the state is the same whichever world is actual, and the act's content is fixed necessarily, which is the modal collapse the argument aims to avoid [W4405407480.arg1.r2]. The dilemma is therefore not conflation of truth-conditions with ontology but a choice about individuation. Your appeal to a necessary desire for a contingent object does not help, because a desire's identity is typically fixed by its object, which is exactly what makes it relational. The extrinsic model of divine knowing [W1967680842.a3] and the truthmaker view [W7172336769.c066] face the same choice. I concede the argument as stated does not establish that every contingent truthmaker makes the property extrinsic; it needs the individuation premise.

objection.text: Consider Ada, a potter who has always been disposed to make bowls and who, on a given morning, freely decides to make a bowl rather than a jug. The proposition 'Ada freely decides to make a bowl' is true. Its truth seems to depend on Ada's standing necessary-looking dispositions, but also on the contingent fact that she has clay and a wheel. Suppose we ask what makes the proposition true. A tempting answer is that the clay fact is merely a condition on what she can act upon, not a truthmaker for the decision itself. Now transfer this to God: 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' is true in virtue of God's will, with the world figuring only as the object willed. The world's contingency enters the content of the proposition (what is chosen) but not its truth-grounds (that God wills it). The proposition is therefore grounded entirely in God's intrinsic volition, and the claimed conjunction of a necessary fact about God with a contingent fact about the world is not required.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise c014 fails because it assumes the truthmaker of 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' must include a contingent worldly fact, when the world figures only in the proposition's content (what is chosen), not in what makes the choice-attribution true.

objection.text: A necessarily existing being named Ash satisfies divine simplicity: every truth only about him has him alone as minimal truthmaker. Ash freely forms the contingent intrinsic intention to create world W. The relational proposition “Ash is the creator of W” is true solely because of that intrinsic contingent volition; W’s existence is an effect, not a partial metaphysical ground. If Ash had refrained, no relation would obtain, yet the relation that does obtain is wholly fixed by a contingent intrinsic fact, with no extrinsic fact partially constituting it.
objection.premise_fails_because: W4405407480.c015 fails because a simple being’s relation to its creation can be wholly grounded in a contingent intrinsic volition rather than in any extrinsic fact.

objection.text: God is absolutely simple—no parts, no accidents, essence identical to existence. Consider the proposition "God is unsurpassable in power." This is non-tautological and only about God: it is a single-subject predication naming no other entity. Yet its minimal truthmaker is not God alone. What makes it true is God plus the fact that no possible being exceeds God's power—a modal-comparative fact about the space of possible beings. If some possible being had possessed greater power, the proposition would be false, so its truthmaker must include the absence of such a being. Divine simplicity is a thesis about God's internal metaphysical composition; it says nothing about what entities serve as truthmakers for truths about God. A simple God can be the truthmaker for "God is powerful" without being the sole truthmaker for "God is unsurpassably powerful."
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise W4405407480.c012 fails because divine simplicity concerns God's internal composition, not truthmaker relations, so it does not require that every non-tautological truth about God has only God as its minimal truthmaker.

objection.text: Imagine a theistic tradition where divine simplicity is defined in purely negative terms (e.g., ‘God is not composite’), and its adherents find modal collapseobjections incoherent because their notion of simplicity lacks the strong truthmaker commitments of premise c012. In this tradition, the modal collapse argument is not even a live issue, as the objection assumes a framework they reject. Thus, the argument’s difficulty is not universal.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise c008 fails because the modal collapse argument is not the most difficult objection for all accounts of divine simplicity.

objection.text: Consider God's accidental property: 'being, at time t, the sole truthmaker of the world's existence.' In a world where God does not create, this property is absent; in our world, it is present. The property is therefore accidental. Now ask: what makes the attribution 'God is the sole truthmaker of the world's existence' correct? The answer is God alone—God's own nature as the creator. No contingent fact 'besides God' enters the truthmaking. The world's existence is not a further truthmaker alongside God; it is what God's truthmaking activity produces, not what constitutes the truth of the attribution. The attribution's truth is fixed by God's being the creator, full stop. Yet c013 insists that any correct attribution of an accidental property to God requires, as truthmaker, 'God and something contingent besides God.' This case shows an accidental property of God whose truthmaker is God alone, with no extrinsic contingent element. The property is accidental without being extrinsically grounded.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise c013 fails because God's accidental property of being the sole truthmaker of the world's existence is correctly truthmade by God alone, with no contingent fact besides God required, contradicting the claim that accidental properties always need an extrinsic contingent truthmaker.

objection.text: Consider a scenario where God's volition to create the world is an intrinsic property, driven by God's own nature and desires. In this case, God's relation to the world is still partially based on facts extrinsic to God, such as the world's existence and properties. However, the accidental property of volition remains intrinsic to God, as it is a fundamental aspect of God's character. This scenario suggests that the connection between God's relation to the world and the nature of accidental properties is not as straightforward as assumed.
objection.premise_fails_because: The hidden premise fails because it incorrectly assumes that God's relation to the world being partially based on extrinsic facts necessarily implies that the accidental properties of volition and knowledge must also be extrinsic.

objection.text: Father John, a parish priest, teaches that God freely chose to create the actual world only because the world could be ordered in a certain way; he says God's will depends on the existence of contingent possibilities. In Thomist thought, God's free act of creation is a simple, non‑composite act whose truthmaker is God alone. The act does not require a contingent fact to be true; it is a necessary act of the divine intellect and will. Hence the proposition ‘God freely chooses to create the actual world’ cannot be true by virtue of a conjunction of a necessary fact and a contingent fact: it is true solely by God’s simple act, independent of any extrinsic condition.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise W4405407480.c014 fails because Thomist classical theism holds that God’s free act of creation is a simple, intrinsic act, not dependent on any contingent fact.

objection.text: Consider a person, Leo, who decides to drink water. The truth of 'Leo decides to drink water' is made true by Leo's internal volition. This volition is a property of Leo. objection.text: Consider a case: God, eternally and without any change in His nature, wills that a certain lamp be lit at noon. The willing is intrinsic to God and grounded wholly in His necessary goodness and power. Now suppose a contingent fact about the world: the lamp's wick happens to be dry. The proposition 'God wills the lamp is lit' is true only if the lamp is lit, so its truthmaker includes a contingent fact about the wick. Yet the volition is not extrinsic in the relevant sense: had the wick been wet, God's willing would be unchanged and only its satisfaction, not the volition, would differ. The premise assumes that any contingent item in a truthmaker makes the property extrinsic, but the property's intrinsic character (the act of willing, individuated by God's nature) is fixed without the wick. The contingent fact enters only the truthmaker of the relational or satisfaction-involving proposition, not of the volition itself. So the antecedent of r1 can hold while the property remains intrinsic.

objection.text: Consider Ada, a potter who has resolved to make one bowl and no other, before any clay exists. Her resolve is fixed by her settled character and plan; the content 'make bowl B' is picked out by her intention alone, and B's specific identity is not yet anything. When clay is delivered, B comes to exist, and the sentence 'Ada made B' becomes true. Her intention did not change; what changed is that a contingent object now satisfies a description her intrinsic intention already determined. The truthmaker of 'Ada made B' includes B, yet the content of her volition, 'make the bowl that suits this plan,' was fixed without reference to any worldly fact. Analogously, God's volition can have a content specified intrinsically, such as 'bring about whatever world satisfies this plan,' with the identity of W entering only in the truth of 'God creates W,' not in the content of the volition. The revised premise conflates the truthmaker of an attribution with the determinant of the volition's content, and the case shows these come apart.
